y-m-64-01.title: Checking Minseo's calculation of counting number tags
y-m-64-01.topic: Counting cases: counting objects that satisfy at least one of two conditions
y-m-64-01.goal: In a solution that counted the objects satisfying at least one of two conditions, find and fix the line that goes wrong, and judge when the same way of calculating is right.
y-m-64-01.material: School lockers are numbered one each from 1 to 40, and all the numbers are different. This week's inspection targets are 'lockers whose number is a multiple of 2 or a multiple of 5'. A locker is a target if it satisfies at least one of the two conditions, and even if it satisfies both, it is counted as 1 locker. Minseo calculated how many targets there are as below.
y-m-64-01.thinking.0: Find the location of the error in the solution
y-m-64-01.thinking.1: Verify the result with another method
y-m-64-01.thinking.2: Judge the conditions under which the same way works
y-m-64-01.prereq.0: 'H1' in this task is only an indicator of difficulty and support level in this production assignment and does not mean the curriculum assigns this subject to a particular school year. It assumes you have already started the counting cases unit of high school Probability and Statistics.
y-m-64-01.prereq.1: The meaning of multiples and the experience of listing and counting numbers from 1 to 40
y-m-64-01.prereq.2: The fact that 'A or B' means 'at least one of the two' (even if both are satisfied, it is 1 target)
y-m-64-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line that goes wrong in Minseo's calculation. (Line numbers are counted from 1.)
y-m-64-01.s.s1.hint.0: Write the list of multiples of 2 and the list of multiples of 5 side by side up to 40.
y-m-64-01.s.s1.hint.1: Find whether the two lists have the same numbers, and count how many times those numbers are included in the 20 + 8 in line 3.
y-m-64-01.s.s1.line.0: Among numbers 1 to 40, the multiples of 2 are 2, 4, …, 40, so there are 20.
y-m-64-01.s.s1.line.1: The multiples of 5 are 5, 10, …, 40, so there are 8.
y-m-64-01.s.s1.line.2: 'A multiple of 2 or a multiple of 5' combines the two cases, so 20 + 8 = 28.
y-m-64-01.s.s1.line.3: So there are 28 lockers to inspect.
y-m-64-01.s.s1.explain: It goes wrong at line 3. If you add the 20 multiples of 2 and the 8 multiples of 5 as they are, the numbers that are in both lists (10, 20, 30, 40) are counted twice. Line 4 simply takes over the result of line 3, so it is wrong too. The counts in lines 1 and 2 are right.
y-m-64-01.s.s2.prompt: Find how many targets there really are, and write, as if speaking to Minseo, why Minseo's 28 must change. You may use any method.
y-m-64-01.s.s2.hint.0: In a small range (numbers 1 to 10), first list the two lists and count directly.
y-m-64-01.s.s2.hint.1: If your answer is not 24, mark in the lists the numbers that were counted twice.
y-m-64-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you say specifically why the count you found differs from 28, and because of which numbers?
y-m-64-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you check your answer once more with another method (for example, counting the numbers that satisfy neither condition and subtracting from the total)?
y-m-64-01.s.s2.model.0: There are 24 targets. If you add the 20 multiples of 2 and the 8 multiples of 5, 10, 20, 30, 40 go in twice, so you must subtract those 4 once each. 20 + 8 - 4 = 24.
y-m-64-01.s.s2.model.1: Among 1 to 40, the numbers that are neither multiples of 2 nor of 5 are 1, 3, 7, 9, 11, 13, 17, 19, 21, 23, 27, 29, 31, 33, 37, 39, so there are 16. So 40 - 16 = 24, and 28 is the value that counted the overlapping numbers.
y-m-64-01.s.s3.prompt: In which case is it still right to calculate the same way (just adding the counts of the two lists)? Choose from the number tags 1 to 40.
y-m-64-01.s.s3.hint.0: For each option, find and write the numbers up to 40 that satisfy both conditions.
y-m-64-01.s.s3.hint.1: Work out whether the first number that is a common multiple of the two numbers is 40 or less.
y-m-64-01.s.s3.o.a: All number tags that are multiples of 3 or multiples of 4
y-m-64-01.s.s3.r.a: 12, 24, 36 satisfy both conditions and are counted twice. This case also needs the overlap checked.
y-m-64-01.s.s3.o.b: All number tags that are multiples of 6 or multiples of 9
y-m-64-01.s.s3.r.b: 18 and 36 satisfy both conditions. If you add as they are, the result comes out that much larger.
y-m-64-01.s.s3.o.c: Number tags that are multiples of 2 or multiples of 8
y-m-64-01.s.s3.r.c: All multiples of 8 are multiples of 2, so very many numbers are counted twice. One list is entirely contained in the other.
y-m-64-01.s.s3.o.d: Number tags that are multiples of 7 or multiples of 11
y-m-64-01.s.s3.r.d: This is a judgment that listed the two lists to the end and checked whether any numbers overlap.
y-m-64-01.s.s3.explain: The multiples of 7 are 7, 14, 21, 28, 35, which is 5, and the multiples of 11 are 11, 22, 33, which is 3, and the two lists have no overlapping number, so adding as they are, 5 + 3 = 8, is fine. In the others there are overlapping numbers, so adding as they are comes out that much larger.

y-m-64-02.title: When two people sit next to each other, what did Doyun's 120 count?
y-m-64-02.topic: Permutations: the number of ways two people sit next to each other
y-m-64-02.goal: Judge first by estimation, find where the solution that counted with a group goes wrong, then explain what the wrong value actually counted and fix the solution.
y-m-64-02.material: Six people (가, 나, 다, 라, 마, 바) sit in a row on 6 numbered chairs. They are all different people, one person sits in each chair, and the number of ways to sit is 6! = 720 in all (6! is read 'six factorial' and is 6×5×4×3×2×1). '가 and 나 are next to each other' means the two sit in adjacent chairs, and it doesn't matter which one is on the left.
y-m-64-02.thinking.0: Estimate the size before calculating the value
y-m-64-02.thinking.1: Find the missing cases in a solution
y-m-64-02.thinking.2: Interpret what a wrong value means
y-m-64-02.prereq.0: 'H1' in this task is only an indicator of difficulty and support level in this production assignment and does not mean the curriculum assigns this subject to a particular school year. It assumes you have met, in high school Probability and Statistics, the number of ways to line up different things in a row.
y-m-64-02.prereq.1: The meaning that n! (n factorial) is the number found by multiplying from n down to 1
y-m-64-02.prereq.2: The experience of listing out all small cases (3 people)
y-m-64-02.s.s1.prompt: Let's estimate before calculating. Out of the 720 ways, about how many have 가 and 나 next to each other? Choose the most appropriate estimate.
y-m-64-02.s.s1.hint.0: Fix the 6 chairs that 가 can sit in one at a time, and write for each chair how many chairs 나 could be next to.
y-m-64-02.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether the number of adjacent chairs is the same for an end chair and a middle chair. Also write how many remaining chairs 나 can sit in after 가 has sat.
y-m-64-02.s.s1.o.a: About one third of the total (around 240 ways)
y-m-64-02.s.s1.r.a: This is a thought that estimated the ratio by counting, for each of 가's chairs, the number of adjacent chairs 나 can sit in.
y-m-64-02.s.s1.o.b: About one sixth of the total (around 120 ways)
y-m-64-02.s.s1.r.b: This is an estimate that looked at only one seat, without counting for each chair 가 sits in how many adjacent chairs are available for 나.
y-m-64-02.s.s1.o.c: About half of the total (around 360 ways)
y-m-64-02.s.s1.r.c: This is an estimate that split into adjacent or not adjacent and took it as half and half. The number of adjacent chairs depends on 가's chair, so the ratio is different.
y-m-64-02.s.s1.o.d: About two thirds of the total (around 480 ways)
y-m-64-02.s.s1.r.d: This may be an estimate that swapped the adjacent case and the non-adjacent case. 가 has at most 2 adjacent chairs.
y-m-64-02.s.s1.explain: If 가 sits at an end chair (2 places), there is 1 adjacent chair for 나, and if 가 sits at a middle chair (4 places), there are 2. After 가 sits, there are 5 chairs 나 can sit in, so the ratio is (2×1 + 4×2) ÷ (6×5) = 10/30 = 1/3, that is, 240 ways.
y-m-64-02.s.s2.prompt: Doyun calculated by treating 가 and 나 as one group. Choose the first line that goes wrong. (Line numbers are counted from 1.)
y-m-64-02.s.s2.hint.0: Write directly on two chairs how the two people inside the group slot can sit.
y-m-64-02.s.s2.hint.1: Check with a small case. When the three people 가, 나, 다 sit in a row, list all the ways 가 and 나 are next to each other, and compare with the value counted the same way.
y-m-64-02.s.s2.line.0: Treat 가 and 나 as one group. The 1 group plus the other 4 people make 5 objects.
y-m-64-02.s.s2.line.1: The number of ways to line up 5 objects in a row is 5! = 120.
y-m-64-02.s.s2.line.2: Inside the group, 가 and 나 are already attached, so the order is not counted separately.
y-m-64-02.s.s2.line.3: So the number of ways 가 and 나 are next to each other is 120.
y-m-64-02.s.s2.explain: It goes wrong at line 3. Inside the group, both orders (가, 나) and (나, 가) are possible, but it was counted as only one. 5! = 120 is the value counting only the cases where 가 sits immediately to the left of 나, and there are just as many cases where 나 sits on the left. Line 4 takes over the result of line 3, so it is wrong too.
y-m-64-02.s.s3.prompt: Is Doyun's 120 a useless value? Explain what cases 120 counted, and correct the number of adjacent cases.
y-m-64-02.s.s3.hint.0: Draw a few of the seating arrangements counted in the 120 ways. Which side are 가 and 나 sitting on?
y-m-64-02.s.s3.hint.1: In the drawings, swap the seats of 가 and 나 and count the new seating arrangements that arise.
y-m-64-02.s.s3.placeholder: Example: 120 is the value counting only the cases where ... So ...
y-m-64-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say what cases 120 counted, even down to which of (가, 나) is on the left?
y-m-64-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check whether the estimated size (about one third of the total) matches the value you corrected?
y-m-64-02.s.s3.model.0: 120 is the value counting only the cases where 가 sits immediately to the left of 나. There are also 120 ways where 나 sits on the left, so together it is 240 ways.
y-m-64-02.s.s3.model.1: Inside the group there are two orders, 가나 and 나가, and 120 counted only one of them. So you have to multiply 5! by 2 and correct it to 240 ways.

y-m-64-03.title: To answer 'In how many ways can we choose 3 of 7 people?', what else do we need?
y-m-64-03.topic: Combinations and permutations: the number of ways of choosing, and the information needed
y-m-64-03.goal: Judge whether a question is sufficient to determine one answer, and explain what information would make the answer determined and how the values are related to each other.
y-m-64-03.material: The math club has 7 members, all different people. The teacher asked, 'In how many ways can we choose 3 people from the 7 members?' It has not yet been said what jobs the 3 chosen people will take.
y-m-64-03.thinking.0: Judge whether the information is sufficient
y-m-64-03.prereq.0: 'H1' in this task is only an indicator of difficulty and support level in this production assignment and does not mean the curriculum assigns this subject to a particular school year. It assumes you have met counting cases in high school Probability and Statistics.
y-m-64-03.prereq.1: The experience of explaining in words the difference between cases where order matters and where it does not when choosing some from different things
y-m-64-03.prereq.2: The experience of listing out and confirming that there are 6 ways to line up 3 people in a row
y-m-64-03.s.s1.prompt: Can the answer be determined as one from this question alone? Choose the most appropriate judgment.
y-m-64-03.s.s1.hint.0: Write in one line each what situation 35, 210, and 343 each count.
y-m-64-03.s.s1.hint.1: Mark which sentence of the question each value comes from. See whether any value uses a condition that is not in the question.
y-m-64-03.s.s1.o.a: It is just choosing 3 of 7 people, so it is determined as 35 ways
y-m-64-03.s.s1.r.a: This reads it as counting only groups of 3 different people. Did you check that even for the same 3 people, if the jobs they take differ, the number of ways increases?
y-m-64-03.s.s1.o.b: If we don't know how the 3 chosen people will be used, it is not determined as one
y-m-64-03.s.s1.r.b: This is a judgment that found where the answer can change and asked for information.
y-m-64-03.s.s1.o.c: It is 3 people lining up, so it is determined as 210 ways
y-m-64-03.s.s1.r.c: The question has neither the words about lining up nor about dividing up posts. Where did you get the condition that order matters?
y-m-64-03.s.s1.o.d: One person can be chosen several times, so it is determined as 343 ways
y-m-64-03.s.s1.r.d: The condition that the same person can be chosen repeatedly is also not in the question. This is also an assumption.
y-m-64-03.s.s1.o.e: The question is ambiguous so we can't say any value, and it is even hard to name candidates
y-m-64-03.s.s1.r.e: Even when information is lacking, you can organize the candidate values (35, 210, 343, etc., depending on the conditions). 'We can't say anything' is giving up too much.
y-m-64-03.s.s1.explain: The question does not say whether the 3 chosen people are given different jobs (whether order matters) or whether one person can take several jobs, so the answer is not determined as one. However, reading 'ways of choosing' as a group of 3 people who are not distinguished is a natural reading, so it is also reasonable to answer 35 ways while stating that assumption.
y-m-64-03.s.s1.acc.0: If we read 'ways of choosing' as a group of 3 people who are not distinguished, it is 35 ways. However, you must also state the assumption that it would change if there were a condition of dividing up posts.
y-m-64-03.s.s2.prompt: Among the following new pieces of information, choose all those that, if given, would determine the answer as one.
y-m-64-03.s.s2.hint.0: Read each piece of information and ask whether it has now been settled 'whether the jobs they take are distinguished' and 'whether one person can take two jobs'.
y-m-64-03.s.s2.hint.1: If it has been settled, calculate the value in that situation yourself. If the calculation does not come out as one, the information is lacking.
y-m-64-03.s.s2.o.a: The 3 chosen people take the posts of president, vice president, and secretary, one each, with no one holding two posts
y-m-64-03.s.s2.r.a: This is a choice that read that the condition cares even about who has which post, so the same 3 people are counted as divided into several cases.
y-m-64-03.s.s2.o.b: The 3 chosen people together take the same cleaning duty
y-m-64-03.s.s2.r.b: This is a choice that read that the condition only requires caring who the 3 people are.
y-m-64-03.s.s2.o.c: Among the 3 chosen people, there is at least one 3rd-year student
y-m-64-03.s.s2.r.c: If we don't know the grade makeup, we can't determine how many ways there are. This information does not settle whether the jobs are distinguished or whether holding two jobs is allowed.
y-m-64-03.s.s2.o.d: Choose a president, vice president, and secretary, and one person may hold several posts
y-m-64-03.s.s2.r.d: This is a choice that read that the condition of choosing one of 7 people for each post is settled.
y-m-64-03.s.s2.o.e: The president is already decided, and we choose the people for the remaining posts
y-m-64-03.s.s2.r.e: We can't tell how many posts remain or whether they are different posts, so it is still not determined as one.
y-m-64-03.s.s2.explain: a gives 7×6×5 = 210 ways, b gives 35 ways as a group of 3 of the 7 different people, and d gives 7×7×7 = 343 ways. c and e do not say whether the jobs are distinguished or whether holding two jobs is allowed, so the answer is not determined.
y-m-64-03.s.s3.prompt: What is the relationship between 35 and 210? Even though the same 3 people are chosen, why are the values different? Explain the relationship between them.
y-m-64-03.s.s3.hint.0: Write out all the ways to arrange 3 people (for example, 가, 나, 다) and count how many there are.
y-m-64-03.s.s3.hint.1: Pick one group from the 35 and count how many times that group is included in the 210.
y-m-64-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say separately what 35 and 210 each count?
y-m-64-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you connect the number of ways to hand out jobs to the same 3 people with the ratio (how many times) between the two values?
y-m-64-03.s.s3.model.0: 35 counts only who the 3 people are, and 210 also counts the cases of handing out different posts to those 3 people. Even for the same 3 people, there are 6 ways to divide up the posts, so 35×6 = 210.
y-m-64-03.s.s3.model.1: If there are no post distinctions, it is 35 ways, and if there are posts, 6 ways of arranging the same three people are added for each, giving 210 ways. So you should first ask whether the question has posts.

y-m-64-04.title: Packing 4 ice cream cups in a box: how many ways?
y-m-64-04.topic: Combinations with repetition: counting all cases without missing any by the number of each flavor
y-m-64-04.goal: In a situation of choosing several of the same thing without caring about order, make all the possible combinations without leaving any out, and explain how it differs from counting where order matters.
y-m-64-04.material: An ice cream shop has three flavors, strawberry, chocolate, and vanilla, and there are plenty of each flavor. You choose 4 cups and put them in one box. You may put in the same flavor several times, and the order in which the cups sit in the box does not matter. That is, 'strawberry 2, chocolate 1, vanilla 1' is the same box however you arrange the cups.
y-m-64-04.thinking.0: Make several combinations that fit the conditions
y-m-64-04.thinking.1: Decide on an order for counting without missing any
y-m-64-04.thinking.2: Explain what a wrong way of counting counts
y-m-64-04.prereq.0: 'H1' in this task is only an indicator of difficulty and support level in this production assignment and does not mean the curriculum assigns this subject to a particular school year. It assumes you have met permutations and combinations in high school Probability and Statistics and are meeting, for the first time, the case where the same thing can be chosen several times.
y-m-64-04.prereq.1: The experience of listing in a table ordered triples whose sum is fixed
y-m-64-04.prereq.2: Expressing counts with integers that are 0 or greater
y-m-64-04.s.s1.prompt: Make 8 different box combinations by the number of each flavor. Strawberry a, chocolate b, vanilla c, and there are 4 cups in all.
y-m-64-04.s.s1.hint.0: First write the boxes that hold only one flavor, 4 cups of it.
y-m-64-04.s.s1.hint.1: Make a table that reduces the strawberry count one at a time, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0, filling in the other two flavors. You can tell how far you have written.
y-m-64-04.s.s1.fail.c1: A count cannot be less than 0.
y-m-64-04.s.s1.fail.c2: A cup can't be split, so the count must be an integer.
y-m-64-04.s.s1.fail.c3: The cups of the three flavors must add up to 4.
y-m-64-04.s.s1.explain: (a, b, c) is the number of each flavor, and every ordered triple of integers that are 0 or greater with sum 4 is a different box. Writing them all gives (4,0,0), (3,1,0), (3,0,1), (2,2,0), (2,1,1), (2,0,2), (1,3,0), (1,2,1), (1,1,2), (1,0,3), (0,4,0), (0,3,1), (0,2,2), (0,1,3), (0,0,4), which is 15 ways.
y-m-64-04.s.s2.prompt: If you write the list you made above all the way through, how many box combinations are there in all? Choose the explanation that fits the list best.
y-m-64-04.s.s2.hint.0: Before counting the number in the list you wrote above, first work out whether each option distinguishes the cups from each other.
y-m-64-04.s.s2.hint.1: Compare whether the value in each option equals the number in the list. If your list is not 15, check where something is missing.
y-m-64-04.s.s2.o.a: 15 ways: all cases of the numbers of each flavor (a, b, c)
y-m-64-04.s.s2.r.a: This is a way of counting that matches the value from writing out the list you made all the way through.
y-m-64-04.s.s2.o.b: 81 ways: for each cup, choose one of the three flavors (3×3×3×3)
y-m-64-04.s.s2.r.b: This is the value that distinguished the cups as first, second, … and counted even the order. In this box, order does not matter.
y-m-64-04.s.s2.r.c: You wrote this expression because the sum is 7, but you did not check with the list above whether it matches the actual number of combinations.
y-m-64-04.s.s2.r.d: This is the value of the number of flavors times the number of cups. This product does not correspond to each box combination.
y-m-64-04.s.s2.explain: Writing the numbers of each flavor (a, b, c) without leaving any out gives 15 ways. 81 is a value that distinguished the cups and counted even the order, so it counted the same box several times, and 35 and 12 do not correspond to the combinations of this box.
y-m-64-04.s.s3.prompt: Why is 81 not the number of combinations for this box? Explain with an example how the same box is included in the 81 ways.
y-m-64-04.s.s3.hint.0: Write out all the ways of the box with strawberry 2, chocolate 1, vanilla 1, distinguishing even the order of the cups. How many come out?
y-m-64-04.s.s3.hint.1: Suppose that number is contained in 81, and compare how many it reduces to as a box combination that doesn't care about order.
y-m-64-04.s.s3.placeholder: Example: 81 is a value that counted ..., so the same box ...
y-m-64-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you give a specific example in which the same box was counted several times in the 81 ways?
y-m-64-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say how many times one box is counted in the 81 ways (for example, strawberry 2, chocolate 1, vanilla 1)?
y-m-64-04.s.s3.model.0: 81 is the value that distinguished the cups as first, second, … and counted even the order. The box with strawberry 2, chocolate 1, vanilla 1 is the same box even if the order of putting them in differs, but in 81 it is counted several times as different ones, so it is much larger than 15.
y-m-64-04.s.s3.model.1: 81 includes cases where the same box was counted several times. This is because it treats (strawberry, chocolate) and (chocolate, strawberry) as different. To keep the agreement that the same numbers of each flavor means the same combination, you should count only the numbers.

y-m-64-05.title: Telling a friend 'the probability of rain on at least one of three days'
y-m-64-05.topic: Addition and multiplication of probabilities, and the independence assumption: the probability of rain on at least one of three days
y-m-64-05.goal: Learn that finding the probability of 'at least one day' from the daily probabilities depends on assumptions about the relationship between events, and tell a friend while stating those assumptions.
y-m-64-05.material: A weather app says 'the probability of rain is 30%' for each of today, tomorrow, and the day after tomorrow. A classmate, Hajun, wants to know 'the probability of rain on at least one of the three days'. At least one day includes all the cases where it rains on 1 day, 2 days, or 3 days.
y-m-64-05.thinking.0: Change your first judgment with new information
y-m-64-05.thinking.1: Bring out the assumptions a calculation result relies on
y-m-64-05.thinking.2: Convey assumptions and values to suit the audience
y-m-64-05.prereq.0: 'H1' in this task is only an indicator of difficulty and support level in this production assignment and does not mean the curriculum assigns this subject to a particular school year. It assumes you have met, in high school Probability and Statistics, the meaning of probability and the probability that an event does not happen.
y-m-64-05.prereq.1: The everyday meaning of the phrase 'they do not affect each other'
y-m-64-05.prereq.2: Converting percentages to decimals and multiplying
y-m-64-05.s.s1.prompt: This is the first judgment. What is the most appropriate value you can tell Hajun?
y-m-64-05.s.s1.hint.0: Instead of listing all the cases where it rains on at least one day, first think about the opposite case (it does not rain on all three days).
y-m-64-05.s.s1.hint.1: Say how to combine the probability that it does not rain today with the probabilities that it does not rain tomorrow and the day after, and what assumption is needed for the way of combining.
y-m-64-05.s.s1.r.a: The days when it rains on all three days are included in each of 'rain today', 'rain tomorrow', and 'rain the day after', so they were counted several times over. Adding makes it bigger than the real value.
y-m-64-05.s.s1.o.b: 30%: the probability is the same every day, so it is the same for three days
y-m-64-05.s.s1.r.b: What would have to happen for the probability of one day and the probability of at least one day out of three to be the same? As days increase, the chances of rain increase.
y-m-64-05.s.s1.o.c: Can't be determined as one: because we don't know the relationship between the days
y-m-64-05.s.s1.r.c: You pointed out that if we don't know the relationship, the value is not determined as one. Still, you can state the range from 30% to 90%.
y-m-64-05.s.s1.o.d: About 65.7%: subtract the probability that it never rains
y-m-64-05.s.s1.r.d: This is a solution that first found the case where it does not rain on all three days and subtracted it from the whole. Did you also think about the fact that it includes the assumption that the days do not affect each other?
y-m-64-05.s.s1.explain: If we regard whether it rains each day as not affecting the others, the probability that it does not rain on all three days is 0.7×0.7×0.7 = 0.343, and the probability of rain on at least one day is 1 - 0.343 = 0.657, about 65.7%. This value rests on the assumption that 'they do not affect each other', and if we don't know the relationship, we can only state the range from 30% to 90%.
y-m-64-05.s.s1.acc.0: The judgment that the value is not determined as one if we don't know the relationship between the days is valid. However, it would be better to state both the range 30% to 90% and the about 65.7% when we assume no influence.
y-m-64-05.s.s2.prompt: This is new information. The weather service's explanation: 'All three days are affected by the same cloud band, so if it rains it rains all three days, and if it doesn't rain it doesn't rain all three days. The probability of rain on each day is still 30%.' After reading this explanation, what is the probability of rain on at least one day?
y-m-64-05.s.s2.hint.0: According to the explanation, first check whether the case 'it rains only today and not tomorrow' is possible.
y-m-64-05.s.s2.hint.1: If the only possible cases are 'rain on all three days' and 'no rain on all three days', look at which of the two the cases of rain on at least one day can be sorted into.
y-m-64-05.s.s2.o.a: About 65.7%: the value found earlier is still right
y-m-64-05.s.s2.r.a: The earlier value rested on the assumption that the days do not affect each other. The explanation changed that assumption.
y-m-64-05.s.s2.o.b: 30%: if it rains on one day, it rains on all three days
y-m-64-05.s.s2.r.b: This is a judgment that read 'at least one day' as the same as 'all three days', so it equals the probability of one day.
y-m-64-05.s.s2.o.c: 90%: if it rains on all three days, the probabilities add up
y-m-64-05.s.s2.r.c: If the three days move completely together, the chances of rain on at least one of the three days do not increase.
y-m-64-05.s.s2.explain: If it rains, it rains for all three days, and if not, it does not rain for all three days, so 'rain on at least one day' is the same event as 'rain on all three days' and its probability is 30%. Even with the same 30% per day, if the relationship between the events differs, the probability of at least one day can vary from 30% to 65.7% to 90%.
y-m-64-05.s.s3.prompt: Write a message to send to Hajun. Include ① the value when the days are regarded as not affecting each other, ② the value when the three days move together as in the explanation, and ③ what each of those values assumes, and write it so your friend understands.
y-m-64-05.s.s3.hint.0: First write ① when there is no influence and ② when they move together on separate lines.
y-m-64-05.s.s3.hint.1: At the end of each line, add 'This value is when we assume ...'.
y-m-64-05.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The probability of rain on at least one of the three days is ...
y-m-64-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write distinguishing which assumption each of the two values comes from?
y-m-64-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you add a word on whether the assumptions are realistic so your friend can judge which value to believe?
y-m-64-05.s.s3.model.0: If we regard rainy days as not affecting each other, the probability of rain on at least one of the three days is 1 - 0.7×0.7×0.7, about 65.7%. But if the three days move together because of the same cloud band, it's only 30%. Weather often continues from day to day, so the assumption of no influence may be a bit optimistic.
y-m-64-05.s.s3.model.1: The probability of rain on at least one day varies with the assumption. If we say they do not affect each other, it is about 0.657 (65.7%), and if the three days come all at once or not at all, it is 30%. So let's decide whether to bring an umbrella by looking at whether the weather is continuing.

y-m-64-06.title: How does the probability change as information is added one piece at a time?
y-m-64-06.topic: Conditional probability: how the probability changes as information is added
y-m-64-06.goal: Follow, by counting cases, how each time new information arrives the possible cases shrink and the probability rises, stays the same, or becomes 1.
y-m-64-06.material: A red die and a blue die are each thrown once. The two dice are fair and do not affect each other, and each face from 1 to 6 comes up with equal probability. If the sum of the two faces is 8 or more, it is called a 'success'. The result is not yet known, and information is given one piece at a time.
y-m-64-06.thinking.0: See how new information changes the possible cases
y-m-64-06.thinking.1: Say the grounds for revising or keeping a judgment
y-m-64-06.thinking.2: Explain why a probability does not change
y-m-64-06.prereq.0: 'H1' in this task is only an indicator of difficulty and support level in this production assignment and does not mean the curriculum assigns this subject to a particular school year. It assumes you have met, in high school Probability and Statistics, the method of finding a probability as (number of cases that happen) ÷ (number of all cases).
y-m-64-06.prereq.1: The experience of listing the faces of the two dice as 36 ordered pairs (red die face, blue die face)
y-m-64-06.prereq.2: The idea of 'keeping only the cases that fit the given information'
y-m-64-06.s.s1.prompt: Information is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose about how large the probability of 'success' is.
y-m-64-06.s.s1.hint.0: Each time you receive information, write the 36 cases in a table, cross out the cells that do not fit the information, and count the remaining cells.
y-m-64-06.s.s1.hint.1: Count the number of remaining cells with sum 8 or more, write the ratio, and compare it side by side with the ratio from the previous step.
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.0.info: This is before throwing. There is no information about the faces yet.
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.0.ask: About how large is the probability of success (the sum of the two faces is 8 or more)?
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.0.after: The cases with sum 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 are 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 ways respectively, so 15 ways in all. The probability is 15/36 = 5/12.
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.0.o.a: About one third (around 12 of the 36 ways)
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.0.r.a: If you write all the cases with sum 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, it is not 12 ways. Check how many ways are missing from which sum.
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is an estimate that took the middle value of the sums, 7, as the dividing line and saw it as half and half. The 6 ways with sum 7 are not successes.
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This matches the value from counting the cases with sum 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 and adding them.
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.0.o.d: About two thirds (around 24 of the 36 ways)
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This may be an estimate that felt '8 or more' is a wide range among the 6 sums (7 to 12). The larger the sum, the fewer the cases.
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.1.info: A student tells you only that 'the sum of the two faces is even'. You still don't know the faces.
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.1.ask: How has the probability of success changed now?
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.1.after: The cases with an even sum are 18 ways (sums 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 have 1, 3, 5, 5, 3, 1 ways respectively), and among them success (sums 8, 10, 12) is 9 ways. The probability is 9/18 = 1/2, which became larger than 5/12.
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This matches the value from counting, among the 18 ways with an even sum, the 5 + 3 + 1 = 9 ways with sum 8, 10, 12.
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It is the same as at first, 5/12
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.1.r.b: The information that the sum is even reduces the possible cases from 36 ways to 18 ways. You need to count again within the reduced cases.
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It became smaller, to about one third
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.1.r.c: If you keep only the cases with an even sum, the share of the cases with sum 8, 10, 12 actually becomes larger. Count the remaining cases yourself.
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.1.o.d: It became much larger, to about 5/6 or more
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.1.r.d: The cases with an even sum also include sums 2, 4, 6. Many cases that are not successes still remain.
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.2.info: The student adds: 'The sum is even, and the faces of the two dice are different from each other.'
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.2.ask: How has the probability of success changed now?
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.2.after: The cases with an even sum and different faces are 18 - 6 = 12 ways, and among them successes are 9 - 3 = 6 ways. The probability is 6/12 = 1/2, staying the same. The 3 success cases (4,4), (5,5), (6,6) were removed together, so the ratio did not change.
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.2.r.a: If you remove the cases where the faces are the same, success cases are removed too. Count how much is removed from each side.
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Check whether you assumed the cases with the same faces are only on the side that is not success. What are the sums of (4,4), (5,5), (6,6)?
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.2.o.c: New information was added, so it must change
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.2.r.c: New information does not always change the probability. Count the remaining cases and check the ratio yourself.
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This is a judgment that counted to check that even when the cases with the same faces are removed, the success cases are also removed at the same ratio.
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.3.info: This is the last piece of information. You are told that the face of the red die is 6. (The sum is even, and the two faces are different.)
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.3.ask: Now what is the probability of success?
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.3.after: If the red face is 6 and the sum is even, the blue face is one of 2, 4, 6, and since the two faces are different, 6 is excluded, leaving 2 or 4. The sum is 8 or 10, both 8 or more, so the probability is 1.
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.3.r.a: Once the face of the red die is fixed, the possible faces of the blue die narrow a lot. Write the remaining cases yourself.
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.3.r.b: This is a judgment that confirmed the remaining cases are only blue faces 2 and 4, whose sums are 8 and 10, both successes.
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.3.r.c: You can check by writing out yourself whether there are any cases that are not success among the remaining cases.
y-m-64-06.s.s1.st.3.r.d: Calculate one by one the sums for the cases where the red face is 6, the sum is even, and the blue face is not 6.
y-m-64-06.s.s1.reflect: The probability changed as 5/12 → 1/2 → 1/2 → 1. Which pieces of information changed the probability, and which did not? Say what happens when information reduces the possible cases and the success cases and the non-success cases shrink at the same ratio.
y-m-64-06.s.s2.prompt: At step 3, the information 'the two faces are different' was added but the probability did not change. Explain why it did not change, using the numbers of remaining cases.
y-m-64-06.s.s2.hint.0: Write the 6 cases removed at step 3 in a table and count how many of them have a sum of 8 or more.
y-m-64-06.s.s2.hint.1: Write 'number of success cases ÷ number of all cases' before and after the removal and compare them.
y-m-64-06.s.s2.placeholder: Example: Even if we remove the cases with the same faces, ...
y-m-64-06.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you say the number of success cases (4,4), (5,5), (6,6) among the removed cases (6 cases with the same faces)?
y-m-64-06.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you put into your own words the point that 'new information does not always change the probability'?
y-m-64-06.s.s2.model.0: Of the 6 cases with the same faces, the ones with a sum of 8 or more are the 3 cases (4,4), (5,5), (6,6), exactly half. Among the 18 ways with an even sum, success was 9 ways, half, so even after removing the 6 same-face cases, success is 6 of the remaining 12 ways, and the ratio stays 1/2.
y-m-64-06.s.s2.model.1: Even if we remove the cases with the same face, the share with a sum of 8 or more among the remaining cases is still half (6/12), so the probability did not change. The new information did reduce the possible cases, but it reduced the success cases and non-success cases at the same ratio.

y-m-64-07.title: The relationship between two events, seen from the membership status of two clubs
y-m-64-07.topic: Independence and mutual exclusivity of events: checking with membership status
y-m-64-07.goal: Confirm, by building membership statuses yourself, that when events are independent there must be cases where they happen together, and explain the conditions under which independence and mutual exclusivity both hold.
y-m-64-07.material: 100 students at a school were surveyed on whether they joined clubs. Event A is 'joined the math club' and event B is 'joined the science club'. Some students may have joined both clubs. When one student is chosen at random, the two events being independent means P(A∩B) = P(A)×P(B), and in terms of numbers of students, 100×(number of students who joined both clubs) = (number of math members)×(number of science members).
y-m-64-07.thinking.0: Rewrite the meaning of independence in numbers
y-m-64-07.thinking.1: Build cases that satisfy the conditions yourself
y-m-64-07.thinking.2: Tell apart the relationship between independence and mutual exclusivity
y-m-64-07.prereq.0: 'H1' in this task is only an indicator of difficulty and support level in this production assignment and does not mean the curriculum assigns this subject to a particular school year. It assumes you have met, in high school Probability and Statistics, the probability of events and the definitions of mutually exclusive events and independent events.
y-m-64-07.prereq.1: Reading probability as the number of students concerned ÷ the total number of students
y-m-64-07.prereq.2: The agreement that two events being independent means P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B)
y-m-64-07.s.s1.prompt: If A and B are independent and each club has at least 1 member, how many students joined both clubs?
y-m-64-07.s.s1.hint.0: Write the meaning of independence as 100×(number who joined both) = (number of math members)×(number of science members), and work out whether the right side can be 0.
y-m-64-07.s.s1.hint.1: If the numbers of math members and science members are both at least 1, look at how large their product is at least.
y-m-64-07.s.s1.o.a: It must be 0: they don't affect each other, so no students overlap
y-m-64-07.s.s1.r.a: You read 'they don't affect each other' and 'they can't happen at the same time' as the same meaning. The two statements are different.
y-m-64-07.s.s1.o.b: It could be 0 or it could be 1 or more
y-m-64-07.s.s1.r.b: You may have judged without rewriting the condition of independence as an equation in numbers of students.
y-m-64-07.s.s1.o.c: There must be at least 1: because the product is not 0
y-m-64-07.s.s1.r.c: This is a judgment that used the fact that, when substituted into the independence equation, the right side is not 0.
y-m-64-07.s.s1.o.d: We can't tell if we don't know the numbers of members
y-m-64-07.s.s1.r.d: Even without knowing the numbers, some things are determined by the properties of the equation alone. Look at whether the product of the two numbers is 0 or not.
y-m-64-07.s.s1.explain: If independent, 100×(number who joined both) = (number of math members)×(number of science members). If both membership numbers are at least 1, the right side is not 0, so the number of students who joined both is also necessarily at least 1. 'Independent' and 'cannot happen at the same time (mutually exclusive)' are different concepts.
y-m-64-07.s.s2.prompt: Make 4 different membership statuses that are independent and in which both clubs have members. Math members x, science members y, both z, and x and y are from 1 to 99. (Statuses with x and y swapped are regarded as the same status.)
y-m-64-07.s.s2.hint.0: First find two numbers x and y whose product x × y is a multiple of 100.
y-m-64-07.s.s2.hint.1: Once you fix x and y, z is determined as z = x × y ÷ 100. Check that z is at most each club's membership and that x + y - z is at most 100.
y-m-64-07.s.s2.ok.c1: The math members and science members are each between 1 and 99.
y-m-64-07.s.s2.fail.c1: x and y must be from 1 to 99.
y-m-64-07.s.s2.ok.c2: The numbers of students are integers.
y-m-64-07.s.s2.fail.c2: The numbers of students must be integers.
y-m-64-07.s.s2.ok.c3: The number who joined both is at least 1 and at most each club's membership.
y-m-64-07.s.s2.fail.c3: The number z who joined both is at least 1 and cannot exceed the smaller of x and y.
y-m-64-07.s.s2.ok.c4: The students who joined do not exceed 100 in total.
y-m-64-07.s.s2.fail.c4: The number of students who joined at least one club (x + y - z) cannot exceed 100.
y-m-64-07.s.s2.ok.c5: It satisfies the condition of independence.
y-m-64-07.s.s2.fail.c5: It is not independent. Check whether 100 × z and x × y are equal.
y-m-64-07.s.s2.explain: For example, with 50 math, 40 science, and 20 both, P(A)=0.5, P(B)=0.4, and P(A∩B)=0.2=0.5×0.4, so they are independent. (20,30,6), (10,10,1), (80,50,40), (60,25,15) are also independent. In all the examples, at least 1 student joined both.
y-m-64-07.s.s3.prompt: Could there be a case where two events are both 'unable to happen at the same time (mutually exclusive)' and 'independent'? Explain with membership statuses.
y-m-64-07.s.s3.hint.0: If mutually exclusive, first write how many students joined both.
y-m-64-07.s.s3.hint.1: Put that value into the independence equation, and work out, when the left side is 0, which of the two probabilities on the right must be 0.
y-m-64-07.s.s3.placeholder: Example: If mutually exclusive, the number who joined both is ...
y-m-64-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: If mutually exclusive, did you first write how many students joined both?
y-m-64-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you substitute into the independence equation and connect that one of the probabilities must be 0?
y-m-64-07.s.s3.model.0: If mutually exclusive, the number of students who joined both clubs is 0, so P(A∩B)=0. If independent, P(A)×P(B)=0 is needed, so only when one of A or B has probability 0, that is, no members at all, can the events be both mutually exclusive and independent.
y-m-64-07.s.s3.model.1: The only time events are both independent and mutually exclusive is when one club has no members. If both have members, independence means there must be overlapping students, so they can't be mutually exclusive.

y-m-64-08.title: Designing a festival dice booth that works out right on average
y-m-64-08.topic: The expected value of a random variable: designing a festival booth
y-m-64-08.goal: Evaluate a rule by the average result instead of the result of one round, and design several different rules yourself within a target range.
y-m-64-08.material: This is a dice booth at the school festival. A player pays an entry fee of f points and throws a fair die once. If a 6 comes up, the player receives a prize of a points (the entry fee paid is not returned), and if any other number comes up, there is no prize. Points are a score used only within the festival and are not money. The booth wants to run with a set average amount that a player loses per round.
y-m-64-08.thinking.0: Evaluate a rule by its average
y-m-64-08.thinking.2: Explain the difference between the result of one round and the average
y-m-64-08.prereq.0: 'H1' in this task is only an indicator of difficulty and support level in this production assignment and does not mean the curriculum assigns this subject to a particular school year. It assumes you have met, in high school Probability and Statistics, the meaning of random variables and expected value.
y-m-64-08.prereq.1: The experience of reading an average as the sum of (prize × probability)
y-m-64-08.s.s1.prompt: The rule of Booth A is an entry fee of 600 points and a prize of 3000 points if a 6 comes up. How can we read the average points a player gets in one round (the average of prize minus entry fee)?
y-m-64-08.s.s1.hint.0: Write the points received when winning and the points received when losing, and write the probability of each.
y-m-64-08.s.s1.hint.1: Gather the values that have probabilities into one line and add up (value × probability). Also check whether you calculated it as the net gain after paying the entry fee.
y-m-64-08.s.s1.o.a: An average loss of 100 points: the average prize is 500
y-m-64-08.s.s1.r.a: This is a judgment that multiplied the prize by its probability to get the average prize and compared it with the entry fee.
y-m-64-08.s.s1.o.b: An average gain of 100 points: the prize is 5 times the entry fee, so the player wins
y-m-64-08.s.s1.r.b: You saw only that the prize is 5 times the entry fee and did not reflect that the probability of getting a 6 is one sixth.
y-m-64-08.s.s1.o.c: An average of 0 points: the rule is fair to the player
y-m-64-08.s.s1.r.c: Work out, using the probability of getting a 6, how many times the entry fee the prize would have to be for it to be fair.
y-m-64-08.s.s1.o.d: We don't know the result of one round, so we can't say the average either
y-m-64-08.s.s1.r.d: Even if you don't know the result of one round, if the probabilities are set, you can calculate the average.
y-m-64-08.s.s1.explain: The average prize is 3000 × 1/6 = 500 points and the entry fee is 600 points, so the average of one round is 500 - 600 = -100 points, that is, a loss of 100 points. In a single round, a 6 might come up and you earn 2400 points, but if you repeat many times it gets close to the average.
y-m-64-08.s.s2.prompt: Design a rule so that a player loses on average between 100 and 300 points in one round. Make 3 rules with different entry fees. (entry fee f, prize a)
y-m-64-08.s.s2.hint.0: Choose an entry fee first, and write as an interval how much smaller than the entry fee the average prize (prize ÷ 6) must be.
y-m-64-08.s.s2.hint.1: Change the prize candidates by 100 points at a time and check whether the average loss falls within 100 to 300.
y-m-64-08.s.s2.ok.c1: The entry fee and prize are in units of 100 points.
y-m-64-08.s.s2.fail.c1: Please set the entry fee and prize in units of 100 points.
y-m-64-08.s.s2.ok.c2: The entry fee is 100 to 1000, and the prize is at most 5000.
y-m-64-08.s.s2.fail.c2: The entry fee must be at least 100 and at most 1000, and the prize must be at most 5000.
y-m-64-08.s.s2.ok.c3: The prize is larger than the entry fee, so it is attractive.
y-m-64-08.s.s2.fail.c3: The prize must be larger than the entry fee for players to be interested.
y-m-64-08.s.s2.ok.c4: The player's average loss is in the range of 100 to 300 points.
y-m-64-08.s.s2.fail.c4: The average loss (entry fee - prize ÷ 6) is not 100 to 300 points. Compare the prize divided by 6 with the entry fee.
y-m-64-08.s.s2.explain: For example, with (entry fee 500, prize 2400), the average prize is 2400 ÷ 6 = 400 and the average loss is 100. (300, 900) has an average loss of 150, and (1000, 4500) has 250. Even with the same entry fee, changing the prize changes the average loss.
y-m-64-08.s.s3.prompt: Pick one of the rules you made, calculate and write how many points a player loses on average in one round, and explain how the result of one round differs from the average.
y-m-64-08.s.s3.hint.0: First write the prize ÷ 6 of your rule, and subtract it from the entry fee.
y-m-64-08.s.s3.hint.1: Write the net gain of a round where a 6 came up and of a round where it did not, and compare them with the average.
y-m-64-08.s.s3.placeholder: Example: If the entry fee is ... and the prize is ..., the average is ...
y-m-64-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you connect the entry fee, prize, and average loss of your rule with numbers?
y-m-64-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain, with the case of getting a 6, that a single round can have a result different from the average?
y-m-64-08.s.s3.model.0: With an entry fee of 500 and a prize of 2400, the average prize is 2400÷6 = 400, so the average is 400 - 500 = -100, that is, you lose 100 points per round. In one round, if a 6 comes up you earn 1900 points and otherwise you lose 500, which differs from the average, but if you play many times it gets close to the average.
y-m-64-08.s.s3.model.1: My design is an entry fee of 300 and a prize of 900. The average prize is 900÷6 = 150, so the expected value is -150, an average loss of 150 points. In one round you might win, but the more you repeat, the closer you get to the average loss.

y-m-64-09.title: Can we treat the number of successes in this situation as repetitions with the same probability?
y-m-64-09.topic: The binomial distribution: situations where the model fits and situations where it does not
y-m-64-09.goal: Judge, situation by situation, what conditions are needed to treat the number of successes in repeated trials as binomial, and confirm with numbers how the calculation result changes when those conditions are broken.
y-m-64-09.material: To regard the number of successes as following a binomial distribution, (1) the number of trials must be fixed, (2) each trial must result in one of two outcomes, success or failure, (3) the probability of success must be the same in every trial, and (4) the trials must not affect each other. We want to check these four conditions in the situations below. A box contains 6 white balls and 4 black balls.

y-m-64-09.thinking.2: Connect the difference in values to the reason when the model is wrong

It assumes you have met, in high school Probability and Statistics, independent trials and the meaning of the binomial distribution (the number of successes counted by repeating a success with the same probability n times).

y-m-64-09.prereq.2: The experience of explaining in words the difference between sampling with and without replacement
y-m-64-09.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the situations below in which the 'number of successes' can be regarded as binomial.
y-m-64-09.s.s1.hint.0: For each option, check the four conditions one by one without missing any. In particular, check whether the probability of success is the same in every trial.
y-m-64-09.s.s1.hint.1: For an option where the probability seems to change, write out yourself how the probability changes after the first trial to check.
y-m-64-09.s.s1.o.a: The number of white balls that come out when you take balls out of the box one at a time, check the color, don't put them back, and take 5 times
y-m-64-09.s.s1.r.a: Each time you take one out, the proportion of white balls in the box changes, so the probability of success in each trial is not constant.
y-m-64-09.s.s1.o.b: The number of successes when a player with a success rate of 0.6 throws 10 free throws under the same conditions, assuming earlier results do not affect later results
y-m-64-09.s.s1.r.b: This is a choice that checked that all four conditions are in the sentence.
y-m-64-09.s.s1.o.c: The number of successes when the same player throws 10 times, following a rule where the next success rate is 0.8 if the previous attempt was a success and 0.4 if it was a failure
y-m-64-09.s.s1.r.c: The probability of success of a trial changes depending on the previous result, so the trials are affecting each other.
y-m-64-09.s.s1.o.d: The number of white balls that come out when you repeat 5 times taking one ball out of the box, checking the color, and putting it back
y-m-64-09.s.s1.r.d: This is a choice that checked that, because the ball is put back, the state of the box is the same each time.
y-m-64-09.s.s1.o.e: The number of questions answered correctly when you guess randomly on all 10 four-choice questions (questions do not affect each other)
y-m-64-09.s.s1.r.e: This is a choice that checked that the probability of getting each question right is the same and they do not affect each other.
y-m-64-09.s.s1.explain: In b, d, and e, the number of trials is fixed, the probability of success in each trial is constant, and the trials do not affect each other. In a, the balls taken out are not put back, so the probability changes with each trial, and in c, the previous result changes the next probability, so the trials affect each other.
y-m-64-09.s.s2.prompt: About how large is the probability that the player in option b (success rate 0.6) succeeds exactly 7 times out of 10?
y-m-64-09.s.s2.hint.0: Write one case with 7 successes and 3 failures and find the probability of that case.
y-m-64-09.s.s2.hint.1: Count how many such cases there are in all (which 7 are the successes), and multiply the probability of one case by that number.
y-m-64-09.s.s2.r.a: This is the probability of just one particular case in which 7 successes and 3 failures come in some particular order. You missed that there are many possible positions for the 7.
y-m-64-09.s.s2.r.b: You multiplied only the probability of 7 successes and did not reflect the condition that the remaining 3 are failures.
y-m-64-09.s.s2.r.c: You mistook the ratio of successes (7/10) for a probability. It is different from the probability of how many of the 10 are successes.
y-m-64-09.s.s2.r.d: This is a value that reflects both the number of ways to choose the positions of the 7 and the probability of 7 successes and 3 failures.
y-m-64-09.s.s2.explain: The number of ways to choose the positions of the 7 out of 10 is 10C7 = 120, and the probability of each is 0.6^7 × 0.4^3 ≈ 0.001792, so adding them gives 120 × 0.001792 ≈ 0.215.
y-m-64-09.s.s3.prompt: For option a (taking 5 without putting the balls back), the probability that all 5 are white balls, calculated with the binomial formula, is 0.6 to the 5th power ≈ 0.078, but when actually worked out it is 6/252 ≈ 0.024. Explain why the two values differ, connecting it to the conditions of this situation.
y-m-64-09.s.s3.hint.0: Write the number of white balls and the total number of balls in the box after a white ball comes out first.
y-m-64-09.s.s3.hint.1: Find the probability that a white ball comes out second and compare it with 0.6.
y-m-64-09.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Since the balls taken out are not put back, ...
y-m-64-09.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you give concrete numbers showing the white balls in the box decreasing each time one is taken out (for example, 6/10 then 5/9)?
y-m-64-09.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain, including the direction, why the binomial formula is larger than the actual value?
y-m-64-09.s.s3.model.0: Because the balls taken out are not put back, the proportion of white balls in the box changes each time one is taken out. The first is 6/10, but if a white ball comes out, the next drops to 5/9, so it can't be 0.6 every time. So the trials are not independent and the binomial formula comes out larger than the actual value.
y-m-64-09.s.s3.model.1: Since the balls are not put back, the makeup of the remaining balls changes, so the probability of success is not constant. When white balls come out in a row, the remaining white balls decrease, so the probability that all 5 are white is smaller than 0.6 to the 5th power.

y-m-64-10.title: Is a higher score really a better result?
y-m-64-10.topic: The normal distribution and standardization: comparing scores
y-m-64-10.goal: Using new data, confirm how to compare scores on different tests by the mean and spread, and that this comparison rests on an assumption about the shape of the distribution.
y-m-64-10.material: The class has 30 students. Minjun got 85 on the math test and 72 on the English test. The full score of both tests is 100. We want to find out in which subject he did relatively better in the class.
y-m-64-10.thinking.0: Hold off on a comparison with insufficient information
y-m-64-10.thinking.1: Compare with standardized values and state the assumption
y-m-64-10.thinking.2: Revise your judgment when new data shakes the assumption
y-m-64-10.prereq.0: 'H1' in this task is only an indicator of difficulty and support level in this production assignment and does not mean the curriculum assigns this subject to a particular school year. It assumes you have met the normal distribution and the mean and standard deviation in high school Probability and Statistics.
y-m-64-10.prereq.1: That the standardized value = (score - mean) ÷ standard deviation tells how many standard deviations away from the mean a score is
y-m-64-10.prereq.2: That the normal distribution curve is a bell shape symmetric on the left and right around the mean
y-m-64-10.s.s1.prompt: Information is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose your judgment about which subject Minjun did relatively better in.
y-m-64-10.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, organize the information you can use in a table, and first work out whether you can compare with that information.
y-m-64-10.s.s1.hint.1: At step 2, write how far each subject's score is from its mean in multiples of the standard deviation, and at step 3, check whether that comparison fits the ranking data.
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.0.info: Minjun's scores are 85 in math and 72 in English. There is no other information.
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.0.ask: In which subject did he do relatively better?
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.0.after: From the scores alone, we cannot know which test was easier or how spread out the students' scores are. A relative comparison needs information like the mean and standard deviation.
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Each test has a different difficulty and different student scores, so you can't compare by the scores alone.
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It might be English: the lower the score, the harder the test may have been
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.0.r.b: It's possible, but from the scores alone we can't know whether the test was hard. There is no information as grounds.
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.0.o.c: We don't know the mean and the spread yet, so it is hard to judge
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You pointed out what information is needed for the comparison.
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It seems like math, but we don't know the test difficulty so we can't be sure
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This is a judgment that took the difference in scores as a clue but held off on being sure.
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.1.info: This class's mean and standard deviation are 70 and 10 for math, and 60 and about 5 for English. A friend guesses that 'in both tests the scores are spread in a bell shape around the mean' (this has not been confirmed).
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now in which subject can we say he did relatively better?
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.1.after: The standardized values are (85 - 70) ÷ 10 = 1.5 for math and (72 - 60) ÷ 5 = 2.4 for English. In terms of how many standard deviations from the mean, English is at a higher position. However, this interpretation rests on the assumption, not yet confirmed, that the score distribution is bell-shaped.
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Math: it is 15 points above the mean, which is ahead of English's 12 points
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You compared only the score differences. The two tests have different spreads of scores, so the same 15 points and 12 points mean different things.
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.1.o.b: English: it is 2.4 standard deviations above, and math is 1.5 above
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This is a judgment that compared how far from the mean as a multiple of the standard deviation, with (72 - 60) ÷ 5 = 2.4 and (85 - 70) ÷ 10 = 1.5.
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The same: both subjects have scores above the mean
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You looked only at the fact that they are above the mean. You did not compare how far above.
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.1.o.d: It looks like English, but the bell-shape statement is a guess, so it is tentative
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This is a judgment that compared with the standardized values but also considered that the assumption about the shape of the distribution has not been confirmed.
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.2.info: The class's ranking data is revealed. In English, 3 of the 30 got 72 or more, and in math, 2 of the 30 got 85 or more. Most English scores are clustered between 55 and 65, and only a few got high scores, so the shape stretches long to the right.
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.2.ask: How should the judgment change now?
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.2.after: If it were bell-shaped (a normal distribution), the share at 2.4 standard deviations or more above the mean is about 0.8%, so there should be about 0.25 of 30 students, but English has 3, so it is hard to regard it as a normal distribution. For math, the share at 1.5 or more is about 6.7%, so about 2 of 30, which matches the actual 2. By ranking, the English 72 is in the top 3 of 30 (10%) and the math 85 is in the top 2 (about 6.7%), so math is at a slightly higher position. The difference is small, so it is possible to say they are 'similar', but the conclusion of the standardized comparison that English is much higher does not match the ranking data.
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Math: fewer people are above, so it is a more advanced position in the class
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This is a judgment that compared positions directly with the ranking data of 2 or more of 30 students.
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.2.o.b: English: the position measured in standard deviations is higher, so it does not change even with the ranking data
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.2.r.b: The interpretation of standardized values rests on the assumption of a bell shape. The ranking data shows that this assumption does not fit for English.
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The standardized comparison for English is hard to trust: the distribution is skewed and does not represent position well
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This is a judgment that pointed out that the assumption the standardized comparison relies on is broken.
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.2.o.d: The ranking data is a coincidence, so ignore it and keep the earlier judgment
y-m-64-10.s.s1.st.2.r.d: The ranking of all 30 students is not a chance part but the data of the whole class.
y-m-64-10.s.s1.reflect: At first only the scores came in, then the mean and standard deviation, and finally the ranking data. How did your judgment change, and what shape did the distribution have to have for the method of comparing by standard deviation to be trustworthy?
y-m-64-10.s.s2.prompt: Write your conclusion for Minjun. Include which subject is at the relatively higher position, the grounds (which of scores, mean and standard deviation, and ranking you used), and the limits of those grounds.
y-m-64-10.s.s2.hint.0: From the ranking data, write what proportion of 30 the top 3 and the top 2 each are.
y-m-64-10.s.s2.hint.1: Compare side by side the number of top students expected from the standardized values and the actual number.
y-m-64-10.s.s2.placeholder: Example: I think ... is at the higher position. The grounds are ...
y-m-64-10.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you say whether your conclusion relied more on the ranking data or on the standardized values, and why?
y-m-64-10.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you write separately the condition under which standardized values can be trusted (the shape of the distribution) and whether this class's English scores keep that condition?
y-m-64-10.s.s2.model.0: I think math is at a higher position in the class. Measured in standard deviations, English is 2.4 above the mean so it looks higher, but the English score distribution is skewed to one side, so that comparison is hard to trust. By ranking, 3 people got 72 or more in English and 2 got 85 or more in math, so math is ahead.
y-m-64-10.s.s2.model.1: By ranking, math looks further ahead. In math only 2 of 30 got 85 or more, and in English 3 got 72 or more. Values calculated from the mean and standard deviation can be trusted only when the distribution is bell-shaped, and English is skewed, so it has limits.
